findings.summary: Wrike combines project and task management with request forms, proofing, workflows, automation, reporting, resource planning, documents, and AI features.
Flexible workflows, custom fields, reports, dashboards, and cross-team organization are its most repeated strengths.
Request forms and guest proofing are especially valuable for creative and service teams handling client review cycles.
Once configured well, it can centralize complex work and replace fragmented status tracking.
The breadth creates a steep learning curve and can feel unintuitive without deliberate onboarding and administration.
Rigid seat minimums, annual billing, feature gates, and upgrade pressure create strong pricing frustration for small teams.
Mobile depth, support quality, and implementation help receive mixed feedback.
Some capabilities still require workarounds or extra tools despite the platform’s large feature surface.
Wrike is described as both intuitive and complex; simple task use starts quickly, while custom workflows and administration take real learning.
Plan packaging changes frequently and must be checked again before any public price or feature comparison.
